---
title: "Migrating Markdown to Quarto 2"
description: "What changes when a document written for Pandoc, CommonMark or GitHub renders under q2, and how to fix each case."
---

## Overview

Quarto 2 reads its own Markdown dialect, qmd. It is close to Pandoc
Markdown, and most documents render unchanged. Where the two differ,
the difference is usually deliberate: Pandoc guesses what you meant
when markup is incomplete, and q2 reports an error instead. A lone
`*` in a paragraph is literal text to Pandoc; to q2 it is an unclosed
emphasis mark, because the next `*` on the page would have paired
with it silently and you would never have noticed.

This page lists what to change in a document that was written for
Pandoc or another Markdown processor, and what to write differently
in new documents. It is organized by what you see: an error that
stops the render, a warning, or output that is quietly different.

If you are an AI agent writing Markdown that q2 will render, this is
the page to read; the examples below are the habits that most often
need unlearning.

## The one rule: a backslash makes any syntax character literal

Any character that qmd uses for markup can be written literally by
putting a backslash in front of it:

``` qmd
costs \$5 and \$10; the engines\' state; see \_quarto.yml;
N \* D; pass \{ a, b \}; a \[bracketed\] note; an \<anonymous\> tag
```

renders as

> costs \$5 and \$10; the engines\' state; see \_quarto.yml;
> N \* D; pass \{ a, b \}; a \[bracketed\] note; an \<anonymous\> tag

The escape is never wrong: `\A` is always a literal `A`, so a
backslash that turns out to be unnecessary does no harm. An escaped
`'` still renders as a typographic apostrophe. The other fix that
is always available is a code span: `` `{ a, b }` `` needs no
escapes at all, and is usually the better choice for text that *is*
code.

## Errors: the render stops

Each of these is reported with a code and a location, and most of
them point at the exact character to escape.

| You wrote | Pandoc | q2 | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `` `a.rs`'s `` (an apostrophe right after a code span, `_x_` or `**x**`) | apostrophe | Q-2-7, unclosed quote | `` `a.rs`\'s `` |
| `the engines' state` (a plural possessive) | apostrophe | Q-2-10, close quote without an open | `engines\'` |
| `_quarto.yml and _brand.yml` (a `_` at a word boundary) | literal | Q-2-5, unclosed emphasis | `\_quarto.yml` |
| `Q-2-*` or `epub_*` (a `*` at the end of a word) | literal | Q-2-12, unclosed emphasis | `Q-2-\*` |
| `$5 and $10`, `$ q2 render` (a `$` that is not inline math) | literal | parse error | `\$5`, or a code span |
| `{ a, b }` or `{python}` in prose | literal | Q-2-41 (braces are reserved for attributes) or a parse error | `\{ a, b \}`, or a code span |
| a lone `` ` `` in prose | literal | parse error | `` \` `` |
| `` `has a ` inside` `` (a code span containing a backtick) | error too | parse error | double the delimiter: ``` ``has a ` inside`` ``` |
| a code block indented four spaces | code block | Q-2-35 | a fenced block |
| `term` / `: definition` (a definition list) | definition list | Q-2-54 | a list or a table |
| `[^1]: First paragraph.` followed by an indented second paragraph | multi-paragraph note | Q-2-35 (the intended code is Q-2-29) | a block footnote, below |

A footnote with more than one paragraph is written as a fenced div whose
label is the reference, instead of Pandoc's indented continuation:

``` qmd
Quarto writes block footnotes as fenced divs [^1].

::: ^1
First paragraph of the note.

Second paragraph of the note.
:::
```

Two things make these easier to find than the table suggests. First,
`q2 render` prints the opening delimiter for every "unclosed" error
("This is the opening quote. If you need an apostrophe, escape it
with a backslash."), not just the end of the block where it gave up.
Second, when one of these is fixed, the parser gets further into the
document and may report the next one; expect a few rounds on a long
document that was never rendered with q2 before.

Word-internal underscores are fine: `snake_case_name` renders as
written. So does a `*`, `_`, `~` or `^` with whitespace on both sides
(`a * b * c`), a `~` before a number (`~16 files`), and a bare `@`
that is not a citation (`` `main` @ `6bee9ebe` ``). Earlier versions
of q2 rejected some of these; if an old document carries escapes for
them, the escapes are harmless.

## Warnings: the render continues, but check the output

| You wrote | Pandoc | q2 | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[text][ref]` and `[ref]: url` (a reference-style link) | link | Q-2-45 / Q-2-46; rendered as literal spans | an inline link `[text](url)` |
| `[REVISED]`, `[x]` outside a task list (bare brackets) | literal | Q-2-49; rendered as a span | `\[REVISED\]`; a code span for `argv[1]` |
| `<anonymous>`, `Vec<String>` (angle brackets in prose) | raw HTML | Q-2-9; passed through as raw HTML, so invisible in the page | `\<anonymous>` for a placeholder; a code span for a type |
| `<br>`, `<details>` (HTML you want rendered) | raw HTML | Q-2-9; passed through, with a warning | `` `<br>`{=html} `` inline; a ```` ```{=html} ```` block for a tag-only line |

## Shortcodes inside code spans and blocks

Shortcodes are expanded inside inline code spans and fenced code
blocks too, on purpose: an include shortcode in a code block pulls a
reusable snippet into it textually. So a document that *quotes* a
shortcode in code, as an example, gets the shortcode's effect instead
of its text: for an include, a Q-17-2 "include file not found" error;
for `{{{< meta title >}}}` or `{{{< env HOME >}}}`, a Q-16-5 warning and
`?meta:title` in the page; for a made-up name, Q-16-3 "Unknown
shortcode". Two ways to keep it literal:

````{.qmd shortcodes="false"}
```{.markdown shortcodes="false"}
{{< include "snippet.qmd" >}}
```
````

turns expansion off for the whole block, and the escaped form with
triple braces

````{.qmd shortcodes="false"}
```markdown
{{{< include "snippet.qmd" >}}}
```
````

keeps one shortcode literal and renders it with the ordinary double
braces. The triple-brace form works in prose and in inline code spans
as well: `` `{{{< meta title >}}}` ``{shortcodes="false"} renders as `{{{< meta title >}}}`.

To *show* the triple-brace form itself, put the same attribute on the
span: `` `{{{< meta title >}}}`{shortcodes="false"} ``{shortcodes="false"} renders its text
verbatim, as `{{{< meta title >}}}`{shortcodes="false"}.

## Quiet differences: no diagnostic

| You wrote | Pandoc | q2 | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Heading` over a line of `===` or `---` (a setext heading) | heading | a paragraph with the underline in it | `# Heading` |
| `#Heading` (no space after the `#`) | heading, in some processors | a paragraph | `# Heading` |

## Things that are the same

Pipe tables, task lists (`- [ ]`, `- [x]`), autolinks in angle
brackets, two-space and backslash line breaks, HTML comments,
footnotes of one paragraph, `$x^2$` and `$$y$$` math, `~sub~`,
`^sup^` and `~~strike~~`, smart quotes and dashes (`--`, `---`,
`...`), nested lists, block quotes, and any Unicode punctuation or
emoji in prose all render as they do in Pandoc.

## Checking a document

`q2 render file.md` reports every problem it finds in a file. For a
whole project, `q2 render --json-errors` writes one JSON record per
diagnostic to stderr, which is easier to tally than the human-readable
report; each record carries the file, the position, and for
"unclosed" errors the position of the opener. The
[error reference](../../errors/index.qmd) has a page per code with
more examples.
